titre: Kiribati Moves the Date Line, January 1, 1995
accroche: On December 31, 1994, Kiribati bends the date line around its territory, which until then had spanned two different days.
contenu_vulgarise:
Before 1995, a Kiribati civil servant posted in the Gilbert Islands and a colleague posted in the Line Islands, at the other end of the same country, did not just live in different time zones: they lived on different days. The archipelago spreads across three island groups on either side of the old date line, with a twenty-three-hour difference between its two ends. Over a week, only four working days coincided on both sides: on the other days, one office was awaiting a reply on a day that, for the other office, had not yet arrived or had already passed.

## The Mechanism

On December 31, 1994, the government of President Teburoro Tito decides to move the date line to the east of the entire national territory rather than through the middle of it. The Line Islands, including the inhabited atoll of Kiritimati, switch from the UTC-10 and UTC-11 time zones to UTC+13 and UTC+14: for their inhabitants, Friday, December 30, 1994 is directly followed by Sunday, January 1, 1995, Saturday having simply vanished from the local calendar. The whole country now finds itself in one and the same day, and Kiritimati becomes the most advanced inhabited point of all the world's time zones: the first place on Earth where each new day begins.

## The Shift

The government of Kiribati does not stop at administrative convenience. In 1997, it renames Caroline Atoll, located in this new time zone, “Millennium Island,” to bolster its claim to see the first sunrise in the world on January 1, 2000. At the end of December 1999, about sixty I-Kiribati artists and about twenty journalists travel there for the celebration, ahead of competing claims from other Pacific islands.

The episode reveals that the date line is nothing like a border fixed by an international treaty, contrary to what its presence on every world map might lead one to believe: it is only the place where time zones, chosen unilaterally by each country, finally meet at a twenty-four-hour difference. A state can therefore bend it around its own territory, in one direction or the other. In 2011, Samoa made the opposite move for the opposite reason: rather than court a tourist symbol, it jumped from the UTC-11 time zone to UTC+13 to align its working days with those of Australia, New Zealand, and China, purely and simply erasing Friday, December 30, 2011 from its national calendar.

repere.texte: On December 31, 1994, Kiribati's Line Islands switch from the UTC-10 and UTC-11 time zones to UTC+13 and UTC+14: Saturday vanishes from the local calendar, with Friday, December 30, 1994 directly followed by Sunday, January 1, 1995.

carte.punch: In 1994, Kiribati moves the date line. A whole day vanishes from the calendar.
carte.idee: Before 1995, Kiribati lived two days at once, twenty-three hours apart between its ends. On December 31, 1994, the country moves the date line eastward: Saturday vanishes from the calendar, and Kiritimati becomes the first inhabited place to see each new day.

quiz.question: Why did Kiribati move the date line in 1994?
choix: To move closer to the time zone of the United States, its main trading partner at the time
Because a United Nations treaty required that a country not span two different days
To anticipate an international revision of the Greenwich meridian planned for the year 2000
Because the country, split across two different days, shared only four working days out of seven between its two halves
quiz.explication: Kiribati spanned both sides of the old date line, with a twenty-three-hour difference between its islands: the administrative offices of the country's two halves shared only four working days out of seven. In 1994, the country moved the line to the east of its territory to unify its calendar: since the line is fixed by no treaty, each state remains free to choose its own time zone.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which day of the week vanished from the Line Islands' local calendar on December 31, 1994?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text states that Friday, December 30, 1994 was directly followed by Sunday, January 1, 1995: it is Saturday that vanished from the Line Islands' local calendar.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did Samoa, in 2011, make the opposite move to Kiribati's in 1994?
choix: To align its working days with Australia, New Zealand, and China
To become the first inhabited place to see the sun rise on the new year
To comply with a United Nations resolution on Pacific time zones
To make up for a shift caused by daylight saving time
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that Samoa jumped from the UTC-11 time zone to UTC+13 to align its working days with those of Australia, New Zealand, and China, rather than to court a tourist symbol as Kiribati did.
